nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What hypotheses were proposed regarding macroinvertebrate community structure?
nodes.answer: The hypotheses proposed that macroinvertebrate community structure will differ across various river sections and be affected by barriers like dams and weirs, as well as seasonal differences in water and sediment concentration levels.
nodes.paragraph: The present study aimed to investigate macroinvertebrate community structure in relation to water and sediment chemistry variables along a subtropical river system (i.e., the Luvuvhu River) in South Africa. Specifically, this study aimed to: (i) examine the macroinvertebrate S community structure and composition across seasons and sites within the Luvuvhu River, and (ii) assess the relation between water and sediment chemistry variables and macroinvertebrate community structure and composition. We hypothesized that macroinvertebrate community structure will differ across various river sections, mainstream lower reaches and tributaries in relation to major barriers such as dams and weirs which will alter river flows and disrupt habitats, and across seasons which would result in differences in water and sediment concentration levels along the river system. Materials and methods Study area The Luvuvhu River originates from the Soutpansberg Mountains, together with its other tributaries. The river flows over a stretch of approximately 200 km from source to its confluence with the Limpopo River at Pafuri, within the Kruger National Park. The Luvuvhu River is situated within the savanna biome, characterised by a hot and wet summer climate, with mild and dry winters.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What species traits were used as a proxy for interspecific competition in the study?
nodes.answer: The species traits used were feeding type, habitat preference, and stream zonation preference.
nodes.paragraph: Interspecific competition As a proxy for interspecific competition, we used the same species traits as Gillmann et al. (2024a): feeding type (competition for food), habitat preference (micro - scale space competition), and stream zonation preference (macroscale space competition). We obtained trait val - ues from the freshwaterecology.info database (Schmidt-Kloiber & Hering 2015), which provides trait affinities on a 10-point scale. We defined competition as the propor - tion of trait overlap between species, indicating similar habitat and food preferences. Using the Gower Similar - ity from the gawdis package in R (v.0.1.5, de Bello et al. 2021), we calculated the trait similarities for each taxa pair per site and year. A lower Gower distance indicates higher similarity and thus higher likelihood of compe - tition. We then summarized these values to the mean Gower similarity per site and year, which we refer as competition in the following. Abiotic data Catchment land use For each sampling site, we quantified the upstream catchment land use following the methodology used by Sch rings et al.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Habitat restoration|Stream habitat enhancement_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the relationship between water quality improvements and broader ecological outcomes?
nodes.answer: The relationship is complex and influenced by additional factors beyond just water quality enhancements.
nodes.paragraph: Ecological Processes (2025) 14:30 It is widely believed that the recovery of benthic inver - tebrate assemblages in Europe has primarily resulted from improvements in water quality (Haase et al. 2023; Sinclair et al. 2024). While water quality enhancements have undoubtedly played a crucial role, the relationship between these improvements and broader ecological out - comes is more complex than it might appear, especially at larger scales. This complexity raises critical questions about additional factors that influence ecological recov - ery. For instance, hydromorphological restoration pro - jects, which aim to restore physical habitat conditions, have shown varying degrees of success (Kail et al. 2015; Lu et al. 2019). While some studies report positive out - comes (e.g., Feld et al. 2018; Li et al. 2018), others find minimal or no improvements beyond the local habitat scale (e.g., Verdonschot et al. 2016; White et al. 2017). This inconsistency highlights a significant challenge: despite substantial advances in wastewater treatment and water quality, hydromorphological restoration often falls short of achieving ecological recovery.
